description: Placing a Remote ID position in time (S-27). Direct Remote ID carries only tenths of a second after the UTC hour; the hour is reconstructed from the receive time. `captured_at` is where the aircraft is placed; `ts` is what the broadcast claims. Network Remote ID cases place an SP flight state using the response timestamp so the provider's clock skew cancels; expected null means the state is not shown.

units.timestamp_tenths: uint16 as on the wire; 65535 = unknown

generated: Expected values computed by knowledge/tools/gen_vectors.py, which runs the old Python implementation (rootxkit/utm @ 484cd228035f) on these inputs. Regenerate rather than edit.
rule: moment = latest instant at seconds_after_hour into some hour that is not after received_at + tolerance + accuracy; age = received_at - moment; age > 1800 s -> clock_ahead (ts = moment + 1 h); age > max_latency + accuracy -> too_old; else broadcast.

cases.name: hour-taken-from-receive-time
cases.why: The broadcast carries only tenths after the hour; the hour is the receiver's. 0.4 s of latency places it 0.4 s before receipt.

cases.name: rollover-broadcast-before-the-hour-heard-after
cases.why: xx:59:59.9 heard at (xx+1):00:00.2 is in hour xx. Taking the receiver's hour naively would place the aircraft 59 minutes in the future.

cases.name: rollover-broadcast-after-the-hour-heard-before
cases.why: The aircraft's clock is 0.6 s ahead of ours across the hour: within the 1 s tolerance, so it is the next hour, not 59 min 59 s ago.

cases.name: late-broadcast-placed-at-its-own-time
cases.why: S-27: 2 s of receiver latency. Placing at receipt would put a 15 m/s aircraft 30 m from where it was, against a 60 m minimum.

cases.name: within-latency-bound
cases.why: 4.9 s old with a 5 s bound: still the broadcast's own time.

cases.name: beyond-latency-bound-too-old
cases.why: 5.2 s old: more than a receiver can plausibly hold a broadcast; placed on arrival, `ts` still what the broadcast said, counted as too_old.

cases.name: latency-bound-exactly
cases.why: Exactly at the bound is inside (the comparison is strictly greater).

cases.name: declared-accuracy-widens-the-latency-bound
cases.why: Accuracy code 10 = 1.0 s; 5.5 s late is within 5 s + 1 s.

cases.name: small-declared-accuracy-does-not-widen-enough
cases.why: Accuracy code 1 = 0.1 s; 5.5 s late is beyond 5.1 s: too_old. The presence pair of the case above.

cases.name: clock-ahead-within-tolerance
cases.why: 0.8 s ahead of the receiver with a 1 s tolerance: believed (GPS time and NTP differ; the field truncates to tenths).

cases.name: clock-ahead-exactly-at-tolerance
cases.why: Exactly 1.0 s ahead is the latest instant allowed: believed.

cases.name: clock-ahead-beyond-tolerance
cases.why: 3 s ahead: the hour choice puts it 59:57 in the past. Anything more than half an hour old is read as 'clock ahead', not as old: placed on arrival, and `ts` is the time the broadcast claims (an hour later).

cases.name: ahead-and-old-told-apart-ahead-2s
cases.why: Up to half an hour either side of the receiver is told apart: ahead is clock_ahead, behind beyond the latency bound is too_old. A steady clock_ahead count usually means the receiving host's own clock is behind.

cases.name: ahead-and-old-told-apart-ahead-29min
cases.why: Up to half an hour either side of the receiver is told apart: ahead is clock_ahead, behind beyond the latency bound is too_old. A steady clock_ahead count usually means the receiving host's own clock is behind.

cases.name: ahead-and-old-told-apart-behind-10s
cases.why: Up to half an hour either side of the receiver is told apart: ahead is clock_ahead, behind beyond the latency bound is too_old. A steady clock_ahead count usually means the receiving host's own clock is behind.

cases.name: ahead-and-old-told-apart-behind-29min
cases.why: Up to half an hour either side of the receiver is told apart: ahead is clock_ahead, behind beyond the latency bound is too_old. A steady clock_ahead count usually means the receiving host's own clock is behind.

cases.name: unknown-timestamp-0xffff
cases.why: 0xFFFF is the standard's 'unknown': placed on arrival, counted as unknown.

cases.name: timestamp-past-the-hour-is-invalid
cases.why: 36000 tenths (3600.0 s) fits the field but is not inside any hour.

cases.name: network-behind-response-placed-on-our-clock
cases.why: The provider's clock is 5 minutes off ours. The state is 2 s behind the response's own timestamp, so it is placed 2 s before our receive time: the provider's skew cancels inside the response.

cases.name: network-ahead-of-its-response
cases.why: A state newer than the response that carries it is impossible on one clock: placed at receipt and noted.

cases.name: network-older-than-max-age-dropped
cases.why: More than 60 s behind its response: not shown as current at all (null).

cases.name: network-no-response-time-recent
cases.why: Without a response timestamp the state's own time is compared with ours, with the same tolerance and latency bounds as a broadcast.

cases.name: network-no-response-time-clock-ahead
cases.why: 2 s ahead of our clock without a response time: placed at receipt.

cases.name: network-no-response-time-too-old
cases.why: 7 s old: shown, but placed at receipt and noted too_old.

cases.name: network-no-response-time-older-than-max-age
cases.why: 61 s old: dropped.
